name: Battle of Karbala
info: On 10 October 680 at Karbala in southern Iraq, the army of the Umayyad caliph Yazid I killed Husayn ibn Ali, grandson of Muhammad, and most of his small party, with consequences for the Second Fitna and for Shia identity.

facts.place: Karbala, a desert plain about 70 kilometres north of Kufa, in modern-day southern Iraq
facts.sides: The forces of the Umayyad caliph Yazid I, under Umar ibn Sa'd with the governor Ubayd Allah ibn Ziyad directing, an army of 4,000, which Shia sources say grew to 30,000; and a small party led by Husayn ibn Ali, whose companions numbered thirty-two horsemen and forty infantrymen in most accounts, and a few hundred in some
facts.outcome: Husayn was killed with most of his family and close companions, and the surviving members of his family were taken captive to Kufa and then to Damascus.

t: Hereditary succession had no precedent in Islamic history, and Yazid's nomination by Mu'awiya was refused by Husayn and by the sons of other prominent companions of Muhammad.
Husayn's companions numbered thirty-two horsemen and forty infantrymen in most accounts, against an army of 4,000 that Shia sources say grew to 30,000.
The battle is central to Shia history and tradition, remembered every year in Muharram and on Ashura, and modern historians still disagree about what Husayn intended.
dyk: Theophilus of Edessa's history, preserved in later Christian chronicles, corroborates the death of Husayn and most of his men at Karbala after suffering from thirst, but appears to say that he was killed by Mu'awiya as the final engagement of the First Fitna.
ev: Ali is assassinated, and his son Hasan signs a treaty handing power to Mu'awiya
Mu'awiya nominates his son Yazid as his successor
Mu'awiya dies, and Yazid demands allegiance from Husayn and other dissidents
Husayn leaves Mecca for Kufa with about fifty men and his family
Husayn is stopped by Kufan troops and camps at Karbala, where a second army arrives
The Kufan army attacks on 10 Muharram, and Husayn is killed with most of his companions
The Tawwabin, who rose in remorse for Husayn's death, are mostly killed at Ayn al-Warda
Mukhtar al-Thaqafi's forces rout an Umayyad army at Khazir, and Ibn Ziyad is slain

sections.background:
After the assassination of the third caliph Uthman ibn Affan in 656, Ali ibn Abi Talib, a cousin and son-in-law of Muhammad, was proclaimed fourth caliph in Medina. Uthman's kinsman Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan, the long-time governor of Syria, denounced Ali's legitimacy. When Ali was assassinated in 661, his eldest son Hasan succeeded him but soon signed a peace treaty that handed power to Mu'awiya, on the condition that Mu'awiya be a just ruler and allow his successor to be chosen through shura (consultation). After Hasan died in 670, his younger brother Husayn became head of the Banu Hashim clan. Ali's supporters in Kufa gave him their allegiance, but he abided by the treaty while Mu'awiya lived.

In 676 Mu'awiya nominated his son Yazid as successor, a move that has been labelled a breach of the treaty. Hereditary succession had no precedent in Islamic history and aroused opposition. Husayn, Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, Abd Allah ibn Umar and Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr, all sons of prominent companions of Muhammad, refused to support it. According to the historians Fitzpatrick and Walker, Yazid's succession, which was considered an "anomaly in Islamic history", changed the government from a consultative form to a monarchy. Before his death in April 680, Mu'awiya warned Yazid that Husayn and Ibn al-Zubayr might challenge his rule, and advised him to treat Husayn with caution and not to spill his blood, since he was the grandson of Muhammad.
sections.forces:
On his accession Yazid told the governor of Medina, al-Walid ibn Utba, to secure allegiance from Husayn and Ibn al-Zubayr, by force if necessary. Husayn declined to pledge allegiance in a private meeting and left for Mecca. There he received letters from pro-Alids in Kufa, who strongly resented Umayyad rule, asking him to lead a revolt. He sent his cousin Muslim ibn Aqil to assess their support. Yazid installed Ubayd Allah ibn Ziyad as governor of Kufa, Ibn Aqil's following dissipated, and his revolt was crushed and he was killed. Husayn left Mecca on 9 September 680 with fifty men and his family, against the advice of Abd Allah ibn Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr.

Near al-Qadisiyyah his caravan was intercepted by about 1,000 men of the Kufan army under al-Hurr ibn Yazid al-Tamimi, and forced to halt in a desolate place. On 2 October 680 Husayn camped at Karbala. The next day another army of 4,000 arrived under Umar ibn Sa'd, governor of Ray. Husayn's companions, according to most accounts, numbered thirty-two horsemen and forty infantrymen; some sources report forty-five horsemen and a hundred foot-soldiers, or a few hundred men in all. Ibn Sa'd's army totalled 4,000, but Shia sources say that more troops had joined it in preceding days, swelling it to 30,000.

On 10 October Husayn appointed Zuhayr ibn al-Qayn to command his right flank, Habib ibn Muzahir the left and his half-brother Abbas as standard bearer. His camp's tents had been tied together and a ditch dug behind them and filled with wood, to be set alight if attacked.
sections.course:
Ibn Ziyad ordered that Husayn and his companions be denied access to the Euphrates. Ibn Sa'd stationed 500 horsemen on the route, and Husayn's camp stayed without water for three days before fifty men led by Abbas reached the river and filled twenty water-skins. Ibn Ziyad, persuaded by Shimr ibn Dhi al-Jawshan, ordered that Husayn give allegiance or be attacked. On the evening of 9 October Ibn Sa'd agreed to wait until morning, and Husayn told his men that they were free to leave under cover of night. Very few did.

After the morning prayer on 10 October both sides took position, and the ditch was set alight. Husayn addressed his opponents, reproached them for abandoning him after inviting him, and asked to leave. He was told he must first submit to Yazid, which he refused. Al-Hurr defected to him. Ibn Sa'd's army fired volleys of arrows, followed by duels in which several of Husayn's companions were killed. Attacks by the Kufan right wing and by Shimr on the left were repulsed, and cavalry attacks followed. Ibn Sa'd ordered all the tents but Husayn's burned, but the flames hindered his own advance for a while.

After noon prayers Husayn's companions were encircled and almost all were killed. His relatives then joined the fighting, and his son Ali al-Akbar, his half-brothers, including Abbas, and other kinsmen were slain. A young child of Husayn's, sitting on his lap, was hit by an arrow and died. Husayn was struck in the mouth by an arrow. Shimr shouted at the hesitating soldiers to kill him; they wounded him, and he was stabbed and decapitated by Sinan ibn Anas.
sections.aftermath:
Seventy or seventy-two people died on Husayn's side, about twenty of them descendants of Abu Talib, the father of Ali. Eighty-eight died in Ibn Sa'd's army, and were buried before he left. Husayn's clothes, sword and baggage were taken, and the women's jewellery and cloaks. Reports give more than sixty wounds on Husayn's body, which was trampled with horses as Ibn Ziyad had instructed, and the bodies of his companions were decapitated. Members of the Banu Asad tribe buried the headless bodies after Ibn Sa'd had gone. Shimr wanted to execute Husayn's only surviving son, Ali Zayn al-Abidin, who was ill and had not fought, but Ibn Sa'd prevented it.

Husayn's family, with the heads of the dead, was sent to Ibn Ziyad and then to Yazid. Both are reported to have poked Husayn's mouth with a stick, which Henri Lammens suggests is a duplication. Yazid is reported to have been compassionate towards the women and Ali Zayn al-Abidin and to have cursed Ibn Ziyad. After a few days the women were compensated for their looted belongings and sent back to Medina.

In Kufa, Alid partisans who felt guilty at having abandoned Husayn formed the Tawwabin under Sulayman ibn Surad, with the slogan "Revenge for Husayn". Of 16,000 who enlisted, only 4,000 assembled, and most, including Ibn Surad, were killed at Ayn al-Warda in January 685. Mukhtar al-Thaqafi then took Kufa and executed those involved in Husayn's death, among them Ibn Sa'd and Shimr. His forces routed an Umayyad army at Khazir in August 686, and Ibn Ziyad was slain. Mukhtar was killed in April 687.
sections.sources:
The primary source of the Karbala narrative is the Kitab Maqtal al-Husayn of the Kufan historian Abu Mikhnaf, who was an adult by 701 and knew many eyewitnesses. Most of them came from Ibn Sa'd's army, since few people from Husayn's camp survived. According to Julius Wellhausen, many regretted their part and embellished the accounts in Husayn's favour to dilute their guilt. Abu Mikhnaf's original seems to be lost, and the extant version has come through secondary sources such as al-Tabari and al-Baladhuri. The sources are mainly historical in nature, in contrast to later literature, which is mainly hagiographical, though early sources contain some miraculous stories.

An early Christian source also reports the battle. The history of Theophilus of Edessa, partly preserved in the chronicles of Michael the Syrian and Theophanes the Confessor, corroborates the death of Husayn and most of his men after suffering from thirst, but appears to say that he was killed by Mu'awiya, not Yazid, as the final engagement of the First Fitna.

Lammens, relying on an official report to Yazid that says the fighting lasted no longer than a siesta, concluded that there was a quick massacre and that the detailed accounts are Iraqi fabrications. Laura Veccia Vaglieri replied that the contemporary accounts together form "a coherent and credible narrative", and Madelung and Wellhausen hold that the battle lasted from sunrise to sunset. Wellhausen thought Yazid's compassion for the family was only for show and put responsibility on Yazid, while Madelung argues that Yazid diverted blame onto Ibn Ziyad.
sections.legacy:
Heinz Halm writes that "There was no religious aspect to Shi'ism prior to 680", and that Husayn's death was the "big bang" that created Shi'ism. The battle gave the pro-Alid political party a distinct religious identity. Shia Muslims commemorate Husayn's death in the ten days of Muharram, culminating on Ashura, with gatherings and processions, and in some places self-flagellation, which many Shia scholars have criticised. The Imam Husayn Shrine at Karbala is holy in Shia Islam, and the Arba'in pilgrimage there is reported to draw up to 40 million people. Shia Muslims believe that Husayn's death was a sacrifice to protect Islam from corruption by tyrannical rulers, that he knew his fate, and that it was divinely ordained.

Historians differ on Husayn's motives. Wellhausen called the revolt premature and ill-prepared, and Halm saw a struggle for leadership between second-generation Muslims. Donner, Hawting and Kennedy see an attempt to regain what Hasan had renounced. Vaglieri and Madelung describe a man moved by religious conviction, and Madelung adds that he did not seek martyrdom and wanted to return when expected support failed. Jafri holds that Husayn aimed from the start at martyrdom to shake the Muslim community.

The battle was used politically soon after. The Abbasids claimed to have avenged Husayn by overthrowing the Umayyads, and the Buyids and Safavids promoted its rituals. In the 20th century Ruhollah Khomeini compared the Shah to Yazid, and Karbala was reinterpreted as a model of resistance. Sufi poets such as Attar and Rumi also wrote of Husayn.

summary: On 10 October 680 at Karbala, Husayn ibn Ali, grandson of Muhammad, was killed with most of his companions by the army of the Umayyad caliph Yazid I. The accounts of the battle are disputed in detail, and it is central to Shia history and tradition.
references: Wilferd Madelung, The Succession to Muhammad: A Study of the Early Caliphate (Cambridge University Press, 1997)
S. M. Jafri, Origins and Early Development of Shi'a Islam (Longman, 1979)
Heinz Halm, Shi'a Islam: From Religion to Revolution (Markus Wiener Publishers, 1997)
Mahmoud Ayoub, Redemptive Suffering in Islam: A Study of the Devotional Aspects of Ashura in Twelver Shi'ism (Mouton Publishers, 1978)
Kamran S. Aghaie, The Martyrs of Karbala: Shi'i Symbols and Rituals in Modern Iran (University of Washington Press, 2004)
Julius Wellhausen, Die religiös-politischen Oppositionsparteien im alten Islam (Weidmannsche Buchhandlung, 1901)
notes: The article has Husayn struck in the mouth by an arrow 'as he went to the river to drink'; I left the river out and wrote only that he was struck in the mouth.

Disputed: Husayn's motives (Wellhausen, Lammens against Vaglieri, Madelung, Jafri); whether the battle was a quick massacre (Lammens) or lasted sunrise to sunset; Yazid's or Ibn Ziyad's responsibility; Theophilus names Mu'awiya as the killer.

Numbers: Husayn's party 32 horsemen and 40 infantry in most accounts (45 and 100 in some, a few hundred in total); Ibn Sa'd 4,000, 30,000 in Shia sources; Husayn's dead 70 or 72; Umayyad dead 88. The article's lead says 'about 72 men' on the journey; I gave 'fifty' for the departure from Mecca as the section says.

Left out: the legends of the Maqtal literature (miracles), the long Shia observances detail, Hezbollah's statement, the Iran-Iraq war, the Albanian and Urdu literature, shamayel paintings (no depiction of any person described); Zaynab's lament.
The article gives Arba'in as up to 40 million and Ashura attendance at 'over 35 million' in Karbala alone; I used only the 40 million figure, hedged 'reported'.
The article says both Ibn Ziyad and Yazid poked Husayn's mouth with a stick; I kept both as 'reported', with Lammens's suggestion of a duplication.
Self-contradictory or thin: article says Husayn left with 'about 72 men' in the lead but 'fifty men' in the journey section; the description of Abbas's death is not in the primary sources.
